title: China–Singapore Naval Cooperation
dek: What official Chinese and Singaporean publications establish about the two navies’ cooperation since 2015, what each government reports was actually done, and where that record stops.
research_question: How is China–Singapore naval cooperation evolving, and what does the public record establish about its scope, depth, and limits?

scope.included: Thirteen publications preserved in IPR’s record from July–October 2026 and seventeen linked official pages from 2015–2025. The preserved records are PLA Daily reports, China defence ministry statements, MINDEF releases and one Xinhua report carried by PLA Daily. The linked pages are eleven MINDEF releases, including a parliamentary reply and a factsheet; one article from MINDEF’s PIONEER magazine; four Chinese reports published on China’s defence ministry website; and one China Military Online report.
scope.excluded: Unpublished activity, media and think-tank commentary, coast guard and non-naval cooperation, photographs and any claim to an exhaustive survey of either government’s reporting.
scope.method: Compare dated official accounts edition by edition. Event dates stay distinct from publication dates. Advance plans stay distinct from closing accounts: an activity counts as reported completed only when a closing or post-exercise account names it. Agreement provisions are followed from commitment to signed instrument to reported use. Chinese evidence is read in the original. Linked pages outside the record are cited by publisher, date and link only.
scope.collection_limits: The preserved record covers July to October 2026. Earlier editions rely on linked official pages checked on October 26 and November 13, 2026 and not preserved by IPR. A fuller Chinese navy account of the 2023 edition was found only on outlets outside IPR’s registered publishers and is not cited. No paid model processing was used. Restricted source text is not reproduced.

overview: Official Chinese and Singaporean publications show a regular, institutionalised and modest naval relationship. The bilateral exercise Maritime Cooperation has been held five times: once in 2015 and every year since 2023, with the host alternating between Singapore and Zhanjiang. Singapore attributes the gap after a planned 2020 edition to a pandemic pause in flagship exercises. Each edition brought one or two ships from each navy for a few days of planning, professional exchange and sea serials. Closing accounts report gunnery for every edition, usually with communications and manoeuvring and search and rescue, and medical evacuation, mine-warfare transits and replenishment approaches in some years. Advance plans promised more: Chinese reports listed a joint surface strike for 2024, 2025 and 2026 and boarding serials for 2024 and 2025, and no closing account reviewed names either. The exercise sits within a 2008 defence agreement, enhanced in 2019. Of its naval-relevant commitments, regular exercising and a ministerial dialogue are documented in use; a secure defence telephone link reached a signed memorandum in 2023 with no reported use; and no instrument was found for the visiting-forces or logistics arrangements. China describes the cooperation as deepening; Singapore places it among many naval partnerships. The record is official self-description. It does not measure interoperability, readiness or strategic alignment.

sections.heading: Five editions compared
sections.intro: Each edition below gives the host, the ships, the dates and the activities that a closing or post-exercise account reports as done. What was announced in advance follows in the next section. Counting the editions from 2015 hides an eight-year gap.

claims.text: Host: Singapore. Ships: the frigate RSS Intrepid and the missile corvette RSS Valiant; the PLA Navy frigate Yulin. Dates: May 20 and May 23–25, 2015. Reported as done: gunnery firings and manoeuvring drills at sea, with exercise planning and combined simulator training ashore. Source: MINDEF’s release on the final day, reporting the exercise concluded.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s May 25, 2015 closing release gives the shore and sea dates.

claims.limits: This is Singapore’s account, issued as the exercise ended. No Chinese account of the first edition was checked.
claims.heading: 2015 · Singapore hosts the first edition

claims.text: Host: Singapore, from Changi Naval Base. Ships: the frigate RSS Intrepid and the mine countermeasures vessel RSS Punggol; the frigate Yulin and the minesweeper Chibi. Dates: April 28 to May 1, 2023. Reported as done: a PLA Navy helicopter landing on RSS Intrepid, gunnery firing, replenishment-at-sea approaches, search and rescue, simulated minefield transits, and communications and manoeuvring drills, with joint planning, professional exchanges and damage-control training ashore. Sources: MINDEF’s closing release of May 1; China Military Online’s May 4 report lists the same core serials and adds medical evacuation.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s May 1, 2023 closing release gives the exercise window; China Military Online gives the same dates.

claims.limits: Both are participants’ accounts; MINDEF’s opening-day release had planned the same serials, so for 2023 the plan and the closing account match. China Military Online is PLA Daily’s English-language site. A longer Chinese navy account was found only on outlets outside IPR’s registered publishers and is not cited.
claims.heading: 2023 · Singapore hosts the second edition

claims.text: Host: China, at Zhanjiang, the first edition held in China. Ships: the frigate RSS Stalwart; the missile frigate Sanya and the minesweeper Hejian, with shipborne helicopters and a marine detachment listed by China in advance. Dates: September 1–5, 2024, with the sea phase on September 3–5. Reported as done: gunnery firing, search and rescue, manoeuvring in formation, voice procedures for simulated firings, a communications exercise, a replenishment-at-sea approach with Sanya and an exchange of sea riders, after a table-top exercise and professional sharing ashore. Source: PIONEER, MINDEF’s magazine, on the final day.

event_period.date_basis: PIONEER’s September 5, 2024 account gives the shore and sea phases; MINDEF’s August 29 release gave the same window in advance.

claims.limits: This is Singapore’s account of its own ship’s exercise. No Chinese closing account of the 2024 edition was reviewed.
claims.heading: 2024 · Zhanjiang hosts the third edition

claims.text: Host: Singapore, from Changi Naval Base. Ships: the frigate RSS Steadfast and the mine countermeasures vessel RSS Bedok; the frigate Xuchang and the minesweeper Chishui. Dates: May 9–16, 2025. Reported as done: a passage through a mine-threat area, naval gunfire at sea targets, and joint search and rescue with medical evacuation, with ship tours, friendly ball games and professional seminars ashore. Source: a PLA Daily report dated May 16 and published on China’s defence ministry website, which says the Chinese ships completed their tasks and sailed for home.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s May 9, 2025 release gives the window; the PLA Daily report describes an eight-day exercise ending on May 16.

claims.limits: This is China’s account. No Singaporean closing release for the 2025 edition was found; MINDEF’s opening-day release is the only Singaporean source reviewed.
claims.heading: 2025 · Singapore hosts the fourth edition

claims.text: Host: China, at Zhanjiang. Ships: one frigate each, RSS Steadfast and the PLA Navy’s Dali. Dates: China’s defence ministry gives September 3–9; MINDEF gives September 5–9. Reported as done: MINDEF lists an exchange of sea riders, gunnery, communications and manoeuvring, joint search and rescue and medical evacuation; China’s defence ministry lists communications, formation movement, live firing, replenishment at sea, joint search and rescue and casualty transfer, with observers exchanged. PLA Daily’s look-back reports eight sea serials, with gunnery at sea targets on September 9 as the focus. The exercise case study examines the two starting dates.

event_period.date_basis: The ministries agree on a September 9 end but differ on the start: China’s defence ministry gives September 3 and MINDEF September 5.

claims.limits: These are official accounts. The two starting dates are preserved rather than reconciled; the case study sets out what each source does and does not explain.
claims.heading: 2026 · Zhanjiang hosts the fifth edition

claims.text: A May 2019 MINDEF release said the two defence ministers had agreed to hold the next edition in 2020. None of the publications reviewed records a 2020 edition. In June 2022 MINDEF said that flagship bilateral exercises had been put on hold by the COVID-19 pandemic, and its 2023 closing release quoted the Singaporean commander calling that edition a resumption after the pandemic restrictions.
claims.limits: Both statements describe a pause in exercises generally. Neither says in terms that a 2020 edition of Maritime Cooperation was cancelled.
claims.heading: 2020: a planned edition and the pandemic pause

claims.text: Singapore describes the 2026 exercise as the fifth edition conducted since 2015. The record supports that count, but four of the five editions fall in 2023–2026. Annual exercising dates from 2023, not 2015.
claims.limits: This is IPR’s reading of the dated releases. It rests on official counts and on the editions found here; MINDEF attributes the pause to the pandemic only in general terms.
claims.heading: “Since 2015” hides an eight-year gap

claims.text: Since 2023 the host has alternated each year: Singapore in 2023, Zhanjiang in 2024, Singapore in 2025 and Zhanjiang in 2026. Before the 2024 edition, a Xinhua report published on China’s defence ministry website stated an aim of a regular mechanism with hosts alternating annually.
claims.limits: Four years make a pattern, not a commitment. The Chinese report stated an aim; this dossier found no published bilateral agreement that fixes the arrangement, and no Singaporean statement of the same aim was reviewed.
claims.heading: Hosts have alternated since 2023

sections.heading: Advance plans and closing accounts
sections.intro: Releases issued before or on an exercise’s first day describe plans. Closing and post-exercise accounts describe what each government says was done. The two lists often differ. A planned serial that a closing account does not name is unconfirmed, not disproved.

claims.text: Before the 2024 edition, a Xinhua report published on China’s defence ministry website said the exercise was held under the annual plan and by mutual consensus. It listed a joint surface strike, replenishment-at-sea positioning, joint search and rescue, and visit, board, search and seizure among the planned sea serials.

event_period.date_basis: The Xinhua report described the planned content on August 29, 2024, before the exercise opened.

claims.limits: This is a pre-exercise plan. It does not say which navy would conduct each serial; Singapore’s account of its ship’s role follows.
claims.heading: China’s 2024 plan listed boarding

claims.text: MINDEF’s pre-exercise release for 2024 planned helicopter cross-deck landings and said RSS Stalwart would observe PLA Navy boarding and mine-clearance serials, which fits China’s listing of boarding and a marine detachment. PIONEER’s account of the completed exercise reports gunnery, search and rescue, manoeuvring, simulated-firing procedures, communications, a replenishment approach and sea riders. It names none of the planned helicopter, boarding, mine-clearance or strike serials.
claims.limits: PIONEER describes the Singaporean ship’s experience and may leave out serials it did not join. No Chinese closing account of 2024 was reviewed, so the planned serials are unconfirmed rather than disproved.
claims.heading: 2024: what was planned and what Singapore reported
2025: the completion account drops three planned serials
claims.text: As the 2025 edition opened, a Xinhua report published on China’s defence ministry website said the sea phase would centre on a joint surface strike, replenishment at sea, joint search and rescue, and visit, board, search and seizure. The PLA Daily completion report names a passage through a mine-threat area, naval gunfire at sea targets, and joint search and rescue with medical evacuation. It does not name the strike, replenishment or boarding serials.
claims.limits: A completion summary is selective; leaving a serial out does not show that it was dropped. MINDEF’s opening-day release listed gunnery, search and rescue and medical evacuation, all of which the Chinese report names.

claims.heading: The planned joint surface strike
claims.text: Chinese advance accounts listed a joint surface strike for 2024, 2025 and 2026. No closing or post-exercise account reviewed for 2025 or 2026 names one. Each reports naval gunfire: PLA Daily’s 2025 completion report names gunfire at sea targets, and its 2026 look-back calls gunnery at sea targets the focus of eight sea serials, with guns firing on the morning of September 9. Singapore’s releases list gunnery for every edition, as conducted or, for 2025, as planned.
claims.limits: Gunfire at sea targets may be how the planned strike was carried out, but no account says so, and IPR does not treat the two as the same serial. For 2024 only the plan and Singapore’s account were reviewed.

sections.heading: Activities and participation
sections.intro: Each edition paired one or two ships from each navy with planning ashore and a set of basic sea serials. The two governments often describe the same serials in different words.

claims.text: As the 2024 edition opened, a Xinhua report published on China’s defence ministry website said that, compared with the two earlier editions, it ran longer, had more serials and involved deeper exchange. It said the two navies were building the exercise series into a signature programme.
claims.limits: This is one participant’s self-assessment. The longer window is consistent with MINDEF’s dates (five days in 2024, four in 2023), but duration and the number of serials do not by themselves measure depth.
claims.heading: China called 2024 longer and deeper

claims.text: The two concluding accounts describe largely the same activity in different terms. China’s defence ministry lists live firing, formation movement, casualty transfer and treatment, and an exchange of observers; MINDEF lists gunnery firings, manoeuvring, medical evacuation and an exchange of sea riders. Both list communications drills and joint search and rescue, with planning ashore, which China’s account calls a tabletop exercise. Only the Chinese accounts list replenishment at sea, ship tours and a deck reception. PLA Daily’s opening report listed a joint surface strike among the planned serials; neither concluding account nor PLA Daily’s September 12 look-back names one.

event_period.date_basis: The accounts cover the whole exercise. China’s defence ministry dates it from September 3 and MINDEF from September 5; both end it on September 9.

claims.limits: The pairing of terms is IPR’s reading; neither government defines its terms. Both lists are official summaries, and their silence on the planned strike serial does not show that it was dropped.
claims.heading: 2026: the same serials in two vocabularies

claims.text: Across the five editions Singapore sent one or two ships: two in 2015, 2023 and 2025, and one frigate in 2024 and 2026. The PLA Navy’s named contribution was one ship in 2015, two in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and one frigate in 2026. The two-ship editions added mine warfare vessels, and in 2024 China also listed shipborne helicopters and a marine detachment. Announced windows ran from four days in 2023 to eight in 2025. The comparable counts establish that Singapore’s ship commitment has stayed at one or two vessels; they do not show a rise in either navy’s ships, although China’s 2024 pre-exercise report stated an aim of expanding the exercise’s scale. The listed serials vary by edition rather than growing steadily.
claims.limits: Ship numbers are one measure. Capability mix, duration and serials changed from edition to edition, personnel numbers are not consistently published, and no reviewed source measures the complexity of a serial. Durations are announced windows. A steady ship count shows neither stagnation nor deepening.
claims.heading: Singapore has sent one or two ships to each edition

sections.heading: Port calls, exchanges and meetings
sections.intro: Beyond the exercise, the record shows logistical port use, multilateral professional events and ministerial meetings. Each is narrower than its headline suggests.

claims.text: MINDEF said the PLA Navy’s 48th escort task force was at Changi Naval Base for a routine technical stop. It added that Singapore regularly facilitates transits, port calls and stopovers by foreign military ships and aircraft.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s October 5 release describes the stop as under way; it gives no arrival or departure dates.

claims.limits: MINDEF presents the stop as routine and in line with its practice for many navies. Its release does not give arrival or departure dates.
claims.heading: October 2026: a technical stop at Changi

claims.text: Xinhua’s report, carried by PLA Daily, on the task force’s October 23 return to Qingdao distinguishes friendly visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar and Malaysia from technical stops at Oman, Kenya, Singapore and other countries.
claims.limits: Both governments use the same category for the Changi call. The label describes the call’s purpose, a logistical stop rather than a ceremonial visit; it does not exclude accompanying contacts, though neither account reports any.
claims.heading: China listed Singapore as a technical stop

claims.text: PLA Daily reported a PLA Navy international cadet leadership camp at Yantai that opened on August 24, 2026. Cadets from Pakistan, Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam and other countries took part. A team from Singapore’s SAFTI Military Institute sailed in the camp’s regatta on August 25–27.

event_period.date_basis: PLA Daily dates the opening to August 24 and the regatta to August 25–27; the camp’s closing date is not given.

claims.limits: This is a multinational event hosted by China, not a bilateral exchange. Singapore’s participation is one team among several, as reported by the host.
claims.heading: August 2026: a multinational cadet camp

claims.text: A China defence ministry report carried by PLA Daily said that China’s defence minister Dong Jun met Singapore’s defence minister Chan Chun Sing at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on September 16, 2026. In that account, Chan called the two militaries’ cooperation in joint exercises, training and personnel development fruitful.

event_period.date_basis: The report is dated the day of the meeting.

claims.limits: This is the Chinese account of a Singaporean minister’s remarks. MINDEF’s own release on the meeting is in IPR’s record but was not admitted by its relevance screen and is not cited here.
claims.heading: September 2026: ministers meet in Beijing

sections.heading: Agreements: commitment, instrument, use
sections.intro: MINDEF traces the first exercise to a Four-Point Consensus of November 2014. The main published framework is a 2008 defence agreement, enhanced in 2019. Each of its naval-relevant provisions can be followed from commitment to signed instrument to reported use. Most stop early.

claims.text: A MINDEF factsheet records that defence ministers Ng Eng Hen and Wei Fenghe signed an enhanced Agreement on Defence Exchanges and Security Cooperation on October 20, 2019, updating the 2008 original. Three of its new areas bear on naval activity: regularising and scaling up bilateral exercises across the army, navy and air force; a Visiting Forces Agreement for troops in bilateral exercises; and a mutual logistics support arrangement. The others are a regular ministerial dialogue, academic exchanges and a bilateral hotline.

event_period.date_basis: The factsheet, published on the day, gives October 20, 2019 as the signing date.

claims.limits: The factsheet lists commitments, not their execution.
claims.heading: 2019: an enhanced defence agreement
The ministerial dialogue: in use
claims.text: MINDEF identifies a regular Defence Ministers’ Dialogue as an initiative under the enhanced agreement and reports three: in June 2022, June 2023 and May 2024. At the first, the ministers committed to resuming flagship bilateral exercises paused by the pandemic. At the third, they backed holding that year’s naval and army exercises in China.
claims.limits: These are Singapore’s accounts. No later dialogue was found in the releases checked, and the 2026 Xiangshan Forum meeting is not described as one in the account cited here.

claims.heading: The hotline: a signed memorandum, no reported use
claims.text: The 2019 factsheet listed a bilateral hotline. On June 1, 2023, with defence ministers Ng Eng Hen and Li Shangfu present, Singapore’s Permanent Secretary for Defence Chan Heng Kee and Lieutenant-General Jing Jianfeng, a deputy chief of the Joint Staff Department of China’s Central Military Commission, signed a memorandum on establishing a secure defence telephone link. MINDEF said both sides would work towards establishing the link for high-level communications.
claims.limits: The memorandum commits the two sides to work towards a link. It is a signed instrument, not evidence that the link exists or has been used, and no publication reviewed here reports it in operation.

claims.text: Followed to its end point, each naval-relevant commitment stops at a different stage. Bilateral exercising reached documented use: an edition every year since 2023, although the promised scaling up does not show in ship numbers. The ministerial dialogue reached documented use in 2022–2024. The hotline reached a signed memorandum in 2023, with no reported use. For the Visiting Forces Agreement and the mutual logistics support arrangement, no signed instrument and no use were found.
claims.limits: This is IPR’s comparison from a bounded check of MINDEF releases and China’s defence ministry website, not a complete search. Not finding an instrument or its use is not evidence that none exists.
claims.heading: Where each commitment stops

claims.text: In a 2023 parliamentary reply, MINDEF described Maritime Cooperation as one of two bilateral exercises with China and noted that Singapore has similar defence agreements with many countries. In 2024 MINDEF named the armies’ Exercise Cooperation alongside it when reporting the third ministers’ dialogue.
claims.limits: This is Singapore’s framing for a domestic audience. The 2023 reply does not name the other exercise, and the 2024 release does not call Exercise Cooperation the other of the two.
claims.heading: Singapore places the exercise among many

sections.heading: How each government describes it
sections.intro: The two governments describe the same activity with different emphases. Neither account is independent of its author.

claims.text: Chinese state outlets describe naval cooperation with Singapore as developing in depth, increasing mutual trust and promoting practical cooperation. China’s defence ministry adds a shared ability to maintain regional peace and stability.
claims.limits: PLA Daily, the defence ministry and Xinhua are all Chinese state outlets. Shared affiliation limits how far their agreement counts as independent confirmation; it does not show that one copied another.
claims.heading: China: deepening cooperation

claims.text: MINDEF presents the exercise as part of a wide network of naval partnerships and of long-standing, warm relations between the two navies. Its releases stress professional exchange rather than strategic purpose. The two governments’ framings differ in emphasis, not in the facts they report, and both can be accurate.
claims.limits: This is Singapore’s self-description; omitting strategic language is not evidence about strategic intent.
claims.heading: Singapore: one partnership among many

claims.text: In 2026 RSS Steadfast took part in RIMPAC alongside navies of 31 nations, the bilateral Singapan exercise with Japan on August 26–28 and then Maritime Cooperation at Zhanjiang. The navy also took part in an ASEAN–India maritime exercise and an ADMM-Plus maritime security exercise in late September.

event_period.date_basis: The releases date RIMPAC from June 25, Singapan to August 26–28, Maritime Cooperation to September 5–9 and the later multilateral exercises to September 21 to October 2.

claims.limits: These are Singapore’s own releases. They show the breadth of the navy’s calendar, not the relative weight Singapore gives to any one partner.
claims.heading: The same frigate, many partners

claims.text: MINDEF’s 2015 release used the word interoperability to describe the purpose of the first edition, and PIONEER’s 2024 account quotes Singapore’s fleet commander on strengthening interoperability. No publication reviewed here measures interoperability or readiness, and this dossier does not claim either.
claims.limits: Stated aims are attributed to their author. The record does not measure interoperability: five short exercises with one or two ships a side neither establish nor rule it out.
claims.heading: Interoperability is MINDEF’s word, not a finding

sections.heading: Where the record runs out
sections.intro: These limits apply to every section.

claims.text: Every source in this dossier is a publication by a Chinese or Singaporean state body. None is independent observation, and none reports operational outcomes beyond the activities each government chose to describe.
claims.limits: Matching accounts from two governments corroborate dates and participants, not quality or effect.
claims.heading: Official accounts only

claims.text: The record shows recurring, small, publicised exercising and routine port access. It does not measure strategic alignment in either direction. In the same months the same Singaporean frigate exercised with the United States, Japan and others; that shows a broad calendar, and neither establishes nor disproves alignment with any one partner.
claims.limits: This is IPR’s interpretation. Unpublished cooperation and intentions neither government states lie outside the record.
claims.heading: The record does not measure alignment

claims.text: This dossier did not review a Chinese account of the 2015 edition or a Chinese closing account of the 2024 edition, found no Singaporean closing release for 2025, and does not cite a fuller Chinese navy account of 2023 carried only by outlets outside IPR’s registered publishers. Personnel numbers are not given consistently. Absence from this dossier is not absence from the record.
claims.limits: The external research was a bounded check of linked official pages on October 26 and November 13, 2026. It was not a comprehensive search.
claims.heading: What this dossier did not review

sections.heading: What the record establishes
sections.intro: Read together, the publications support a bounded but substantive conclusion.

claims.text: China–Singapore naval cooperation has become regular. After a single edition in 2015 and an eight-year gap that Singapore attributes to a pandemic pause, Maritime Cooperation has been held every year since 2023, with the host alternating between Singapore and Zhanjiang. What the two navies report having done is consistent and basic: one or two ships a side, a few days of planning and exchange ashore, and at sea gunnery in every edition, usually with communications and manoeuvring and search and rescue, and medical evacuation, mine-warfare transits and replenishment approaches in some years. From 2024 on, advance plans listed more than the closing accounts report. A joint surface strike planned for 2024, 2025 and 2026 and boarding serials planned for 2024 and 2025 appear in no closing account reviewed; that does not establish whether they took place. The cooperation rests on a 2008 defence agreement enhanced in 2019. Its exercise and ministerial-dialogue commitments are documented in use; the hotline stops, in the publications reviewed, at a 2023 memorandum to work towards a link; and no instrument was found for the visiting-forces or logistics arrangements. Ship numbers have stayed at one or two a side. Limited published evidence of outcomes is not evidence that the cooperation lacks depth. The record supports describing an established and regular naval exercise relationship, small in the ships committed and basic in its reported serials, framed by China as deepening and by Singapore as one of many naval partnerships.
claims.limits: This is IPR’s synthesis of official publications. It describes what was published, not what was achieved, and would change with Chinese closing accounts of the 2024 edition, Singaporean accounts of 2025 or evidence of the agreement’s other provisions in use.
claims.heading: Regular and institutionalised, with modest demonstrated depth

changes.summary: First release. Machine-assisted draft prepared from thirteen preserved records and nine linked official pages; Benjamin Yang approved the reviewed manuscript at draft digest 5ec6b7feddfc75bd971cb150265e432e803afc487e391a811d09223cbe1d9b5e. Source use is limited to attribution, dates, independent IPR paraphrases and links.

Revision 2. The edition findings become a five-edition comparison of host, ships, dates and activities reported as done, from closing accounts. A new section separates advance plans from closing accounts: the planned joint surface strike and boarding serials appear in no closing account reviewed. The agreements section follows each naval-relevant 2019 commitment to a signed instrument and reported use, adding the 2023 telephone link memorandum and the ministerial dialogues. The 2020 gap cites Singapore’s pandemic explanation. Eight linked official pages are added (x10–x17). No finding is removed; two 2024 plan findings move to the new section.
